Standard papers on this problem were written by Graham [1961] for the Pilansberg dykes in South Africa and by Cox [1961] for lava flows of Plio-Pleistocene age in Idaho's Snake River Plain. They both found that typical lightning strike, with a peak line current of about 22,000 A, would produce a cylindrical zone of anoma- lous magnetization with a radius of about 60 cm. They sug- gested that a minimum field of 0.5 mT is required to produce a lasting IRM. Curves for the strengths of lightning-induced fields attained at various distances from the discharge point of such a strike were given by Cox [1961, p. 155]. Fission track apatite ages determined for all of the other intrusive units fall between 95.9 and 101.4 Ma. Where fission track apatite and sphene ages were determined for the same sample, the apatite ages were always younger, suggesting that there were two periods of intrusion. The silicate units were emplaced during the first event, the carbonates during the second [Eby, 1987]. According to Erickson and Blade [1963] the Magnet Cove complex is zoned concentrically. Its core consists mainly of carbonatite. Its rings comprise trachytes and syenites. Masses of magnetite-rich pyroxenite (jacupirangite), the most mafic rock unit of the suite, occur along the northeastern margin of the complex. Small leucocratic dikes cut all major units. Based on these field relations, Erickson and Blade [1963] proposed the following age sequence, from oldest to youngest: (1) phonolite and trachyte, (2) jacupirangite, (3) alkalic syenites, (4) ijolite, and (5) carbonatite and minor dike rocks. This procedure was suggested independently by Creer et al. [1959] and by Cox [1959]. In a series of masterly papers, Cox [1962, 1964, 1970] then went on to model the effects of dipole wobble and nondipole field vari- ations and compared them with his own and others' observa- tions of the paleosecular variation, bringing PSV analysis into the state we know it today. Another of Cox's contributions was to the study of the magnetic effect of lightning strikes. When lightning strikes, the current passes along the surface carrying with it a transient magnetic field, which induces a strong magnetization termed \"isothermal remanent magnetization\" (IRM). Such effects were bothersome to early mountaineers in Europe because they deflected magnetic compasses, and it is not surprising there- fore that they became the first manifestation of IRM to be studied. With the resurgence of interest in the remanent mag- netism of rocks in the 1950s, such effects were discovered not only in mountainous areas but also in level terrain where the incidence of electrical storms is high. Standard papers on this problem were written by Graham [1961] for the Pilansberg dykes in South Africa and by Cox [1961] for lava flows of Plio-Pleistocene age in Idaho's Snake River Plain. Why then is a reinvesti- gation necessary ? There are three reasons. First, studies of mid-Cretaceous rocks in the western North American Cordilleran and in the Arctic regions are now very numerous, and it is becoming increasingly desirable to know the reference paleopole as ac- curately and reliably as possible in order to make accurate tectonic reconstructions. Second, the mid-Cretaceous is be- coming recognized as an interval during which widespread remagnetization of older rock units commonly occurred. Such effects were bothersome to early mountaineers in Europe because they deflected magnetic compasses, and it is not surprising there- fore that they became the first manifestation of IRM to be studied. With the resurgence of interest in the remanent mag- netism of rocks in the 1950s, such effects were discovered not only in mountainous areas but also in level terrain where the incidence of electrical storms is high. Standard papers on this problem were written by Graham [1961] for the Pilansberg dykes in South Africa and by Cox [1961] for lava flows of Plio-Pleistocene age in Idaho's Snake River Plain. They both found that typical lightning strike, with a peak line current of about 22,000 A, would produce a cylindrical zone of anoma- lous magnetization with a radius of about 60 cm. They sug- gested that a minimum field of 0.5 mT is required to produce a lasting IRM. Curves for the strengths of lightning-induced fields attained at various distances from the discharge point of such a strike were given by Cox [1961, p. 155]. The province lies between the displaced continental fragment of Arctic Alaska and the accreted terranes of southern Alaska. Although Lower Cretaceous volcanogenic rocks of the Yukon-Koyukuk province preserve pri- mary remanent magnetizations, the primary component is masked by a pervasive overprint. The over- printing magnetization, which has dual polarity, was acquired after a Late Cretaceous orogeny left the region highly deformed. By fitting planes to tilt-corrected thermal demagnetization data and solving for the best intersection of the corresponding remagnetization circles, we separated the primary component, presumably a vestige of the original thermoremanent magnetization, from the overprinting component of the natural remanence. The primary magnetization corresponds to a mean paleopole of Early Cretaceous age at 60.2N, 159øE. The mean paleolatitude is 69øN with the 95% confidence ellipse ranging from 60 ø to 75N. This analysis was successful because the tilt corrections of the sampled strata had sufficient variation to ensure a strong intersection of the remagnetization circles. c Rocks We examined thin sections of several representative rock types from the Lower Cretaceous volcanogenic sequence. In some exam- ples, such as the pillow basalt at site 5, the original plagioclase crystals have been replaced by epidote and calcite. The province lies between the displaced continental fragment of Arctic Alaska and the accreted terranes of southern Alaska. Although Lower Cretaceous volcanogenic rocks of the Yukon-Koyukuk province preserve pri- mary remanent magnetizations, the primary component is masked by a pervasive overprint. The over- printing magnetization, which has dual polarity, was acquired after a Late Cretaceous orogeny left the region highly deformed. By fitting planes to tilt-corrected thermal demagnetization data and solving for the best intersection of the corresponding remagnetization circles, we separated the primary component, presumably a vestige of the original thermoremanent magnetization, from the overprinting component of the natural remanence. c Rocks We examined thin sections of several representative rock types from the Lower Cretaceous volcanogenic sequence. The pillow basalt, tuffs, andesite flows, and volcaniclastic rocks have all retained their primary textures, but the rocks also show alteration by low-grade metamorphism. In some exam- ples, such as the pillow basalt at site 5, the original plagioclase crystals have been replaced by epidote and calcite. Chlorite and epidote are pervasive throughout the volcanic sequence. The thin sections show no evidence of penetrative defor- mation, such as grain dislocations or stretching. T indicates the magnetic saturation of magnetite (Figure 4). A slight rise in the IRM curves beyond 0.2 T is due to a high coercivity mineral, probably hematite in low concentration. Most of these rocks were, however, too weakly magnetized to be measured with the fluxgate spinner magnetometer available or were too unstable to give any reliable results. Hard and stable remanence was found only in the quartz porphyry dikes which are closely associated with the rapakivi granites and have a radiometric U-Pb age about 1630 Ma. The magnetization found evi- dently represents the direction of the geomagnetic field prevailing during the late phase of the evolution of the rapakivi magma. The calculated paleomagnetic pole site (30° N, 175° E with »normal» polarity) agrees well with those previously reported for rocks of about the same age in the Baltic Shield. Excellent end-points are found by both af and thermal demagnetization in these 12 cores. d et al., 1982]. The pluton intrudes most stratigraphic units in the center of the southern Burin Peninsula (Figure 2) and cuts all deformation features which they exhibit (thrust faults, folds, cleavage); that is, the St. Lawrence Granite is clearly posttectonic. Its con- tacts are sharp, with chilled quartz-feldspar porphyry margins and hornfelsing of the country rock. Miarolitic cavities occur near contacts, and tuffisites (gas breccias) are common, indi- cating the shallow nature of the intrusion. The rock consists of quartz, orthoclase and albite, with minor amounts of riebeckite, aegirine, biotite, fluorite, mag- netite, and hematite. Alkali feldspar makes up to 30 to 60% of the rock, and is generally turbid with finely disseminated he- matite. Although some joint surfaces are slickensided, their consistent mutually perpendicular orientations, together with the continuity into the country rock of undeformed cogenetic flourspar veins, indicate that the pluton has not been signifi- cantly deformed or tilted since solidification. Tilting is always an important problem in paleomagnetic studies of intrusions and we shall return to it later. The pluton shows evidence of alteration at both high and low temperatures. The pluton intrudes most stratigraphic units in the center of the southern Burin Peninsula (Figure 2) and cuts all deformation features which they exhibit (thrust faults, folds, cleavage); that is, the St. Lawrence Granite is clearly posttectonic. Its con- tacts are sharp, with chilled quartz-feldspar porphyry margins and hornfelsing of the country rock. Miarolitic cavities occur near contacts, and tuffisites (gas breccias) are common, indi- cating the shallow nature of the intrusion. The rock consists of quartz, orthoclase and albite, with minor amounts of riebeckite, aegirine, biotite, fluorite, mag- netite, and hematite. Alkali feldspar makes up to 30 to 60% of the rock, and is generally turbid with finely disseminated he- matite. Although some joint surfaces are slickensided, their consistent mutually perpendicular orientations, together with the continuity into the country rock of undeformed cogenetic flourspar veins, indicate that the pluton has not been signifi- cantly deformed or tilted since solidification. Tilting is always an important problem in paleomagnetic studies of intrusions and we shall return to it later. The pluton shows evidence of alteration at both high and low temperatures. As we shall see, we believe this is caused by Kiaman overprinting which preferentially affected the more superficial rocks. Paleo- zoic rocks require detailed alternating field (af) or thermal demagnetization studies of each specimen (10 or more steps) to separate the magnetizations present. d et al., 1982]. The pluton intrudes most stratigraphic units in the center of the southern Burin Peninsula (Figure 2) and cuts all deformation features which they exhibit (thrust faults, folds, cleavage); that is, the St. Lawrence Granite is clearly posttectonic. Its con- tacts are sharp, with chilled quartz-feldspar porphyry margins and hornfelsing of the country rock. Miarolitic cavities occur near contacts, and tuffisites (gas breccias) are common, indi- cating the shallow nature of the intrusion. The rock consists of quartz, orthoclase and albite, with minor amounts of riebeckite, aegirine, biotite, fluorite, mag- netite, and hematite. Alkali feldspar makes up to 30 to 60% of the rock, and is generally turbid with finely disseminated he- matite. Although some joint surfaces are slickensided, their consistent mutually perpendicular orientations, together with the continuity into the country rock of undeformed cogenetic flourspar veins, indicate that the pluton has not been signifi- cantly deformed or tilted since solidification. Tilting is always an important problem in paleomagnetic studies of intrusions and we shall return to it later. The pluton shows evidence of alteration at both high and low temperatures. As we shall see, we believe this is caused by Kiaman overprinting which preferentially affected the more superficial rocks. Paleo- zoic rocks require detailed alternating field (af) or thermal demagnetization studies of each specimen (10 or more steps) to separate the magnetizations present. Separation of low and intermediate stability magnetizations have been obtained by calculation of the magnetization removed (vector differences) along linear trajectories in the orthogonal plots. Components of very high stability, when present, have been recognized by their stable end-points. We have preferred to get detailed re- sults from comparatively small collections rather than less de- tailed results from larger collections. They are considered to be correlative with the Calmer basalts [Strong et al., 1978b]. They occur on the beach east and west of Famine Back Cove, with an exposed thickness of 15 m. They were sampled through their thickness over a distance of 1 km. The magnetization of three cores is univectorial (Figures 5 and 6). It remains little changed in alternating fields up to 100 mT and temperatures up to 650øC, and it points to the southeast with intermediate downward inclination. The basalts have un- dergone intense deuteric alteration and hematite is the main carrier of the magnetization. In nine cores there is also a substantial (PEF) component, aligned close to the present earth's field, that is removed at low temperatures or after treatment in low alternating fields. Excellent end-points are found by both af and thermal demagnetization in these 12 cores. The remaining three cores have not only PEF and SE magnetizations, but also very small magnetizations sometimes pointing south sometimes north. These very small components could not be accurately isolated (Figure 7). The northerly ones could be overprints acquired at the time of intrusion of the St. Lawrence Granite (see

d et al., 1982]. The pluton intrudes most stratigraphic units in the center of the southern Burin Peninsula (Figure 2) and cuts all deformation features which they exhibit (thrust faults, folds, cleavage); that is, the St. Lawrence Granite is clearly posttectonic. Its con- tacts are sharp, with chilled quartz-feldspar porphyry margins and hornfelsing of the country rock. Miarolitic cavities occur near contacts, and tuffisites (gas breccias) are common, indi- cating the shallow nature of the intrusion. The rock consists of quartz, orthoclase and albite, with minor amounts of riebeckite, aegirine, biotite, fluorite, mag- netite, and hematite. Alkali feldspar makes up to 30 to 60% of the rock, and is generally turbid with finely disseminated he- matite. Although some joint surfaces are slickensided, their consistent mutually perpendicular orientations, together with the continuity into the country rock of undeformed cogenetic flourspar veins, indicate that the pluton has not been signifi- cantly deformed or tilted since solidification. Tilting is always an important problem in paleomagnetic studies of intrusions and we shall return to it later. The pluton shows evidence of alteration at both high and low temperatures. Samples from the alteration zone plot on the same 360 Ma Rb/Sr isochron as the unaltered granite samples, showing that the high temperature alteration is coeval with the granite [Strong et al., 1984]. STRONG Pacific Geoscience Centre, Sidney, British Columbia, Canada Department of Earth Sciences, Memorial University, St. John's, Newfoundland, Canada The posttectonic St. Lawrence Granite (360 + 5 Ma) and associated subvertical dikes have two mag- netizations, N and H. N points north with an intermediate upward inclination (declination, 005 ø' incli- nation, -50 ø' alpha (95), 10 ø' paleopole 12øN, 120øE). We consider N to have been acquired close to the time of initial cooling. The H magnetization points south with low inclination. H is also the dominant magnetization in the nearby Permo-Carboniferous Spanish Room Formation. H is considered to be an overprint acquired chemically during the Kiaman Reversed Superchron (Late Carboniferous and Per- mian). The N magnetization corresponds to a paleolatitude of 31 + 7øS, very different from the near- equatorial values expected from the commonly accepted Late Devonian and earliest Carboniferous (Tournaisian) reference paleofields for cratonic North America. This is generally consistent with the hypothesis of a southerly displaced Acadia proposed by Kent and Opdyke, although the displacement is much greater (30 ø rather than 15ø). However, we show that all inclinations observed from Middle to Upper Devonian and T

dies show small departures of only a few degrees (with one exception based on limited sampling and two from the Colorado Plateau which may have been rotated) which could be caused by experimental inaccuracies. Moreover the directions obtained from cratonic studies are 97% reversed, as they are in rocks with Kiaman magnetizations. We suggest, therefore, that the commonly accepted Late Devonian to earliest Carboniferous reference paleofield for North America is either entirely Kiaman in age or has been seriously affected by Kiaman overprinting. Consequently, the 30 ø of southerly displacement which the N magnetization of the St. Lawrence Granite apears to indicate, and the 15 ø invoked by Kent and Opdyke, we consider to be illusory. Three Late Precambrian rock units (623 to 606 Ma) have scattered declinations but similar inclinations yielding paleolatitudes of about 35 ø. The scattered declinations presumable were caused by local pre- Carboniferous relative rotations. There is little or no evidence of Kiaman overprinting in Precambrian rocks, indicating that overprinting is comparatively superficial and is probably related to Late Paleozoic groundwater circulation. The Avalon Zone, of which the Burin Peninsula is part, extends intermittently from Newfoundland to Florida. Its rock sequences have been compared to similar sequences of North Africa and western Europe [Schenk, 1971; Rast et al., 1976; Strong, 1978], and it could therefore be a fragment of the eastern continents left behind by the Mesozoic opening of the Atlantic [Wilson, 1966]. They are considered to be correlative with the Calmer basalts [Strong et al., 1978b]. They occur on the beach east and west of Famine Back Cove, with an exposed thickness of 15 m. They were sampled through their thickness over a distance of 1 km. The magnetization of three cores is univectorial (Figures 5 and 6). It remains little changed in alternating fields up to 100 mT and temperatures up to 650øC, and it points to the southeast with intermediate downward inclination. The basalts have un- dergone intense deuteric alteration and hematite is the main carrier of the magnetization. In nine cores there is also a substantial (PEF) component, aligned close to the present earth's field, that is removed at low temperatures or after treatment in low alternating fields. Excellent end-points are found by both af and thermal demagnetization in these 12 cores. The remaining three cores have not only PEF and SE magnetizations, but also very small magnetizations sometimes pointing south sometimes north. These very small components could not be accurately isolated (Figure 7). The northerly ones could be overprints acquired at the time of intrusion of the St. Lawrence Granite (see

d et al., 1982]. The pluton intrudes most stratigraphic units in the center of the southern Burin Peninsula (Figure 2) and cuts all deformation features which they exhibit (thrust faults, folds, cleavage); that is, the St. Lawrence Granite is clearly posttectonic. Its con- tacts are sharp, with chilled quartz-feldspar porphyry margins and hornfelsing of the country rock. Miarolitic cavities occur near contacts, and tuffisites (gas breccias) are common, indi- cating the shallow nature of the intrusion. The rock consists of quartz, orthoclase and albite, with minor amounts of riebeckite, aegirine, biotite, fluorite, mag- netite, and hematite. STRONG Pacific Geoscience Centre, Sidney, British Columbia, Canada Department of Earth Sciences, Memorial University, St. John's, Newfoundland, Canada The posttectonic St. Lawrence Granite (360 + 5 Ma) and associated subvertical dikes have two mag- netizations, N and H. N points north with an intermediate upward inclination (declination, 005 ø' incli- nation, -50 ø' alpha (95), 10 ø' paleopole 12øN, 120øE). We consider N to have been acquired close to the time of initial cooling. The H magnetization points south with low inclination. H is also the dominant magnetization in the nearby Permo-Carboniferous Spanish Room Formation. H is considered to be an overprint acquired chemically during the Kiaman Reversed Superchron (Late Carboniferous and Per- mian). The N magnetization corresponds to a paleolatitude of 31 + 7øS, very different from the near- equatorial values expected from the commonly accepted Late Devonian and earliest Carboniferous (Tournaisian) reference paleofields for cratonic North America. This is generally consistent with the hypothesis of a southerly displaced Acadia proposed by Kent and Opdyke, although the displacement is much greater (30 ø rather than 15ø). However, we show that all inclinations observed from Middle to Upper Devonian and T

dies show small departures of only a few degrees (with one exception based on limited sampling and two from the Colorado Plateau which may have been rotated) which could be caused by experimental inaccuracies. Moreover the directions obtained from cratonic studies are 97% reversed, as they are in rocks with Kiaman magnetizations. We suggest, therefore, that the commonly accepted Late Devonian to earliest Carboniferous reference paleofield for North America is either entirely Kiaman in age or has been seriously affected by Kiaman overprinting. Consequently, the 30 ø of southerly displacement which the N magnetization of the St. Lawrence Granite apears to indicate, and the 15 ø invoked by Kent and Opdyke, we consider to be illusory. Three Late Precambrian rock units (623 to 606 Ma) have scattered declinations but similar inclinations yielding paleolatitudes of about 35 ø. The scattered declinations presumable were caused by local pre- Carboniferous relative rotations. There is little or no evidence of Kiaman overprinting in Precambrian rocks, indicating that overprinting is comparatively superficial and is probably related to Late Paleozoic groundwater circulation. The Avalon Zone, of which the Burin Peninsula is part, extends intermittently from Newfoundland to Florida. Its rock sequences have been compared to similar sequences of North Africa and western Europe [Schenk, 1971; Rast et al., 1976; Strong, 1978], and it could therefore be a fragment of the eastern continents left behind by the Mesozoic opening of the Atlantic [Wilson, 1966]. d. Famine Back Cove Basalt. Fifteen cores were drilled from flat-lying reddish amygdaloidal basalts. They are considered to be correlative with the Calmer basalts [Strong et al., 1978b]. They occur on the beach east and west of Famine Back Cove, with an exposed thickness of 15 m. They were sampled through their thickness over a distance of 1 km. The magnetization of three cores is univectorial (Figures 5 and 6). It remains little changed in alternating fields up to 100 mT and temperatures up to 650øC, and it points to the southeast with intermediate downward inclination. The basalts have un- dergone intense deuteric alteration and hematite is the main carrier of the magnetization. In nine cores there is also a substantial (PEF) component, aligned close to the present earth's field, that is removed at low temperatures or after treatment in low alternating fields. Excellent end-points are found by both af and thermal demagnetization in these 12 cores. d et al., 1982]. The pluton intrudes most stratigraphic units in the center of the southern Burin Peninsula (Figure 2) and cuts all deformation features which they exhibit (thrust faults, folds, cleavage); that is, the St. Lawrence Granite is clearly posttectonic. Its con- tacts are sharp, with chilled quartz-feldspar porphyry margins and hornfelsing of the country rock. Miarolitic cavities occur near contacts, and tuffisites (gas breccias) are common, indi- cating the shallow nature of the intrusion. The rock consists of quartz, orthoclase and albite, with minor amounts of riebeckite, aegirine, biotite, fluorite, mag- netite, and hematite. Alkali feldspar makes up to 30 to 60% of the rock, and is generally turbid with finely disseminated he- matite. Although some joint surfaces are slickensided, their consistent mutually perpendicular orientations, together with the continuity into the country rock of undeformed cogenetic flourspar veins, indicate that the pluton has not been signifi- cantly deformed or tilted since solidification. Tilting is always an important problem in paleomagnetic studies of intrusions and we shall return to it later. The pluton shows evidence of alteration at both high and low temperatures. Received 1985 November 4; in original form 1985 April 19 Summary. A palaeomagnetic study of the Moulin de Chateaupanne formation reveals two characteristic components of magnetization. Multicomponent magnetizations of the Snowy River Volcanics have been resolved into pre-folding (dec. = 340.1', inc.= -59.2') and post-folding (dec. = 10.5', inc. = -72.3") elements. The former is attributed to initial cooling of the volcanics while the latter is probably related to the waning stages of the deformational episode which was presumably accompanied by cooling. We argue that the pole position from the pre-folding magnetizations (lat. = 74.3"S, long, = 222.7"E) represents the Australian palaeopole for the early Devonian. A reassessment of other Australian pole positions determined from rocks of about this age suggests that remagnetization during the Carboniferous may be common. Interpretation of the pole path prior to the Devonian is equivocal and awaits further study. The post-folding magnetizations from the volcanics are similar in stability and direction to those from the Buchan Caves Limestone (dec. = 27.8', inc. = - 75.6"), which appears to be completely remagnetized. Multicomponent magnetizations of the Snowy River Volcanics have been resolved into pre-folding (dec. = 340.1', inc.= -59.2') and post-folding (dec. = 10.5', inc. = -72.3") elements. The former is attributed to initial cooling of the volcanics while the latter is probably related to the waning stages of the deformational episode which was presumably accompanied by cooling. We argue that the pole position from the pre-folding magnetizations (lat. = 74.3"S, long, = 222.7"E) represents the Australian palaeopole for the early Devonian. A reassessment of other Australian pole positions determined from rocks of about this age suggests that remagnetization during the Carboniferous may be common. Interpretation of the pole path prior to the Devonian is equivocal and awaits further study. The post-folding magnetizations from the volcanics are similar in stability and direction to those from the Buchan Caves Limestone (dec. = 27.8', inc. = - 75.6"), which appears to be completely remagnetized. The age of this remagnetizing event appears to be mid-Carboniferous if our interpretation of the pole path for this time is correct. It is noted that a muc

ssment of other Australian pole positions determined from rocks of about this age suggests that remagnetization during the Carboniferous may be common. Interpretation of the pole path prior to the Devonian is equivocal and awaits further study. The post-folding magnetizations from the volcanics are similar in stability and direction to those from the Buchan Caves Limestone (dec. = 27.8', inc. = - 75.6"), which appears to be completely remagnetized. The age of this remagnetizing event appears to be mid-Carboniferous if our interpretation of the pole path for this time is correct. It is noted that a much unappreciated attribute of the fold test lies with identifying not just the relative age of magnetization, but also the palaeohorizontal. Only when the palaeohorizontal is established can the calculation of a palaeopole be justified. Using more recently acquired results from Australian rocks, with updated structural information and new age constraints for some rock units previously studied, Goleby (1980) provides a fourth interpretation of the Gondwana Palaeozoic APWP. There is a clear need for a concerted effort t

o investigate the thermal effects of the intrusion on the host rock and to assess the originality of magnetizations present within the intrusion. It is rare that rock outcrop permits the required spread of sampling and generally it is far easier to implement the fold test (Graham 1949). Of itself, a positive contact test does not identify the palaeohorizontal, and therefore does not necessarily justify the calculation of a palaeo- magnetic pole position. Granted, the full contact test when fully executed can prove the originality of magnetization, but without further evidence for the palaeohorizontal the use of magnetizations to infer palaeopole positions may not be valid. In terranes where the remagnetization of rock units is widespread, the opportunity to sample specifically with a fold test in mind is often readily available. In this study we have sampled folded early Devonian rock formations from the Lachlan Fold Belt (LFB) of south- eastern Australia to redress, in part, the shortcomings of the existing results. P. W. Because reversals of the geomagnetic field were frequent in the Late Triassic, it is not possible to determine the hemisphere or origin, so the net displacement since the Late Triassic could have been something in excess of 1000 km from northern palaeolatitudes or 5000 km from southern palaeolatitudes. Determinations of relative displacement critically depend on the accuracy with which the reference palaeopoles of the craton are known. Recent revisions of the geological time-scale (Harland er al. 1952; Kent & Gradstein 1985) have transferred what used to be the main source of Late Triassic reference information (the Newark Supergroup) from the Late Triassic into the Early Jurassic. Moreover, palaeopoles from older (Early Jurassic) and from younger (Middle Jurassic) Newark rocks are significantly different, showing that the earlier Jurassic was an interval of rapid apparent polar movement (Smith & Noltimier 1979). Received 1987 June 10; in original form 1987 January 7 SUMMARY Results of palaeomagnetic and rock magnetic studies are reported mainly for quartz porphyry collected at 18 sites from an Ordovician igneous-sedimentary succession at Tourmakeady and Glensaul in'Co. Mayo, Eire. Both magnetite and haematite are shown to be prominent magnetic constituents. The magnetite is usually in the form of large multidomain grains; these are held responsible for a soft remanence component (called the B-magnetization) with D, Z=OOO, +75; ag5=3.70, i.e. practically identical to the direction of the present axial geocentric dipole field in the area. Hence, it is inferred that the B-magnetization, which is dominant at most sites, is of recent origin. Haematite, which has a more patchy occurrence, apparently formed .through high-temperature oxidation of magnetite. Haematite is the main carrier of the palaeomagnetically significant component, the A-magnetization, which gave well-grouped in situ directions (29 samples from 10 sites) with a mean value of D, I = 182", +6", corresponding to a north pole at 31" N, 169"

dy arc shows that the A-magnetization is of post- folding age. An earlier suggestion that the rocks represent a Lower Ordovician extrusive suite is discussed and discounted. It is inferred that the quartz porphyries constitute syntectonic intrusions having formed during the Taconic orogeny. These rocks as well as their characteristic magnetization are therefore regarded as late Ordovician in age. It is concluded that a c. SO" relative clockwise shift between the mid-Ordovician and late Ordovician-Silurian geomagnetic field axes, previously demonstrated for Scotland, has now been recognized also in Ireland. Key words: Palaeomagnetism, rock magnetism, Ordovician, W. Ireland 1 INTRODUCTION Ordovician rocks in the British Isles have provided some useful palaeomagnetic data for estimating the extent of a Proto-Atlantic ocean. Such tests tend to be difficult, however, since they require exact comparisons between synchronously magnetized rocks from opposite sides of a collision suture. Ireland north of the proposed suture (e.g. Phillips et af. 1976) is one area where previous Ordovician palaeomagnetic work led to conflicting interpretations. Part of the difficulty arose from the considerable tectonic flexuring in Connemara (Dewey 1963) which accompanied the suggested closure of t

le that other palaeomagnetic signatures observed in that region are the result of tectonic distortion. The question is important in the context of Caledonian palaeomagnetism, and in this paper we report results for two Ordovidian inliers exposed at Glensaul and Tourmakeady along a tectonic arc in Connemara (Fig. 1). Between Glensaul and Tourmakeady the regional structure changes from its roughly W-E trend in western Connemara to a SW-NE trend that continues northeastwards roughly along strike with major structures in northern Britain. In a $previous palaeomagnetic study of the Glensaul inlier, Morris (1976) obtained a SW-directed remanence and attributed its c. 30" misalignment with the characteristic British 'N-S' vector to the bending of an SW-NE structure originally assumed to be linear into its present shape. carrier_investigation_candidates.excerpt: Both magnetic and sun compasses were used to orientate a total of 160 sample-blocks from Itajai, Castro and Bom Jardim Groups from sites shown in Fig. 1. Particulars of sampling sites (which were generally quames and roadcuts) are illustrated in Table 1. Site CA-111, within the Campo Alegre Formation, is a quarry which is cut by a vertical rhyolite dyke 35 cm wide which has been sampled. For the Vargas Formation, each sedimentary sample represents a stratigraphic level. Generally four specimens were cut from each rock sample, making a total of 640 which were measured with a spinner magnetometer. Samples were submitted to AF and thermal demagnetization and practically all the specimens, especially those from the Bom Jardim Group, were given a complete pilot treatment. Magnetizations were analysed with the aid of stereonets, Zijderveld diagrams and intensity curves. Fisher's statistics were used for calculating mean values and precision parameters. Site CA-111, within the Campo Alegre Formation, is a quarry which is cut by a vertical rhyolite dyke 35 cm wide which has been sampled. For the Vargas Formation, each sedimentary sample represents a stratigraphic level. Generally four specimens were cut from each rock sample, making a total of 640 which were measured with a spinner magnetometer. Samples were submitted to AF and thermal demagnetization and practically all the specimens, especially those from the Bom Jardim Group, were given a complete pilot treatment. Magnetizations were analysed with the aid of stereonets, Zijderveld diagrams and intensity curves. Fisher's statistics were used for calculating mean values and precision parameters. For the Vargas Formation, each sedimentary sample represents a stratigraphic level. carrier_investigation_candidates.excerpt: Both magnetic and sun compasses were used to orientate a total of 160 sample-blocks from Itajai, Castro and Bom Jardim Groups from sites shown in Fig. 1. Particulars of sampling sites (which were generally quames and roadcuts) are illustrated in Table 1. Site CA-111, within the Campo Alegre Formation, is a quarry which is cut by a vertical rhyolite dyke 35 cm wide which has been sampled. For the Vargas Formation, each sedimentary sample represents a stratigraphic level. Generally four specimens were cut from each rock sample, making a total of 640 which were measured with a spinner magnetometer. Samples were submitted to AF and thermal demagnetization and practically all the specimens, especially those from the Bom Jardim Group, were given a complete pilot treatment. Magnetizations were analysed with the aid of stereonets, Zijderveld diagrams and intensity curves. Fisher's statistics were used for calculating mean values and precision parameters. Particulars of sampling sites (which were generally quames and roadcuts) are illustrated in Table 1. Site CA-111, within the Campo Alegre Formation, is a quarry which is cut by a vertical rhyolite dyke 35 cm wide which has been sampled. carrier_investigation_candidates.excerpt: Both magnetic and sun compasses were used to orientate a total of 160 sample-blocks from Itajai, Castro and Bom Jardim Groups from sites shown in Fig. 1. Particulars of sampling sites (which were generally quames and roadcuts) are illustrated in Table 1. Site CA-111, within the Campo Alegre Formation, is a quarry which is cut by a vertical rhyolite dyke 35 cm wide which has been sampled. For the Vargas Formation, each sedimentary sample represents a stratigraphic level. Generally four specimens were cut from each rock sample, making a total of 640 which were measured with a spinner magnetometer. Samples were submitted to AF and thermal demagnetization and practically all the specimens, especially those from the Bom Jardim Group, were given a complete pilot treatment. Magnetizations were analysed with the aid of stereonets, Zijderveld diagrams and intensity curves. Fisher's statistics were used for calculating mean values and precision parameters. (1982a) have suggested, from geological evidences, an Upper Pre-Cambrian age for the Vargas Formation lithologies, which are older than the other units already described (Castro Group-CT pole, Campo Alegre FormationXA pole, Acampamento Velho Formation-AV1 pole). However, the position of the VA pole related to the curve of Fig. 13 suggests a secondary origin for this component. An yet younger age (Devonian) may be possible if the VA pole is compared with the Middle-Upper Palaeozoic Gondwana APWP's. 5.6 Hilsirio FormatiowHi pole The andesitic samples from Lavras do Sul region, after thermal treatment, presented only one direction of magnetization, which led to the Hi pole of Table 2. The comparison with the curve of Fig. 13, suggests an age of about 750-800 Myr for this direction, which is older than the estimated age for this volcanic episode (700-600Ma; Fragoso Cesar et al. 1982a). 6 CONCLUSIONS This article presents palaeomagnetic results for several geological units related with the Brasiliano-Pan
